King | Ficus skytinodermis | Summerh. | Ficus taeda | Kunth & C.D.Bouché | Urostigma circumscissum | Miq. | Urostigma karet | Miq. | Urostigma odoratum | Miq. }} |synonyms_ref = }} '''''Ficus elastica''''', the '''rubber fig''', '''rubber bush''', '''rubber tree''', '''rubber plant''', or '''Indian rubber bush''', '''Indian rubber tree''', or '''rambung''' is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Moraceae]], native to eastern parts of [[South Asia|South]] and [[Southeast Asia]].{{cite web |url=http://efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200006353 |title=''Ficus elastica'' |author=Zhengyi Wu, Zhe-Kun Zhou & Michael G. Gilbert |work=Flora of China |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden, St. Louis, MO & Harvard University Herbaria, Cambridge, MA |access-date=29 August 2013 |archive-date=20 April 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170420113944/http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2 |url-status=live }} Its common names reflect its historical use as a source of rubber within its native range, but it is not used in the modern commercial-scale production of [[natural rubber]]. ==Description== {{more citations needed section |date=May 2025}} ''Ficus elastica'' is a large tree in the [[banyan]] group of figs, growing to {{cvt|30|–|40|m|ft|round=5}} – rarely up to {{cvt|60|m|ft|round=5|disp=or}} – tall, with a stout trunk up to {{cvt|2|m|ftin}} in diameter. The trunk develops [[Aerial root|aerial]] and [[Buttress roots|buttressing roots]] to anchor it in the soil and help support heavy branches.{{Cite web |title=Brisbane Council Weed Identification Tool |url=https://weeds.brisbane.qld.gov.au/weeds/indian-rubber-tree}} It has broad shiny oval leaves {{cvt|10|–|35|cm|in|frac=2}} long and {{cvt|5|–|15|cm|in|frac=2}} broad; leaf size is largest on young plants (occasionally up to {{cvt|45|cm|in|disp=or|frac=2}} long), much smaller on old trees (typically {{cvt|10|cm|in|0|disp=or}} long). The leaves develop inside a sheath at the apical [[meristem]], which grows larger as the new leaf develops. When it is mature, it unfurls and the sheath drops off the plant. Inside the new leaf, another immature leaf is waiting to develop. The canopy of the tree is dense. ==Pollination and fruiting== As with other members of the genus ''[[Ficus]]'', the flowers require a particular species of [[fig wasp]] to pollinate it in a co-evolved relationship. These wasps enter receptive female flowers by way of the osteole, and deposit their eggs in the female flowers, resulting in pollination.{{Cite web |title=Useful Tropical Plants |url=https://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=ficus+elastica}} Because of this relationship, the rubber plant does not produce highly colourful or fragrant flowers to attract other pollinators. The fruit is a small yellow-green oval fig {{convert|1|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}} long, barely edible; these are fake fruits that contain fertile seeds only in areas where the [[pollinating]] insect is present. ==Range== The natural range of ''F. elastica'' extends from [[Nepal]] in the north to [[Indonesia]], [[Bhutan]], [[Northeastern India]], [[Bangladesh]], [[Myanmar]], [[Thailand]], [[Yunnan]] in [[China]], and [[Malaysia]]. It has been widely introduced in most tropical regions of the world, including in the Americas. In Europe it can be found in mild locations throughout the [[Mediterranean Basin]].{{Cite web |title=Anthemion Flowers: care tips for ficus plants |url=https://anthemionflowers.com/attica_en/blog/post/ficus?srsltid=AfmBOopntggsitP-hlGnEXnv12eoFCC7vkEWQhWnKqEHZKhWn5fOcNH2}} In the Near East, it is a common landscaping element on the streets of Tel Aviv, Israel.{{Cite web |title=Top Twenty Most Common Trees in Tel Aviv |url=https://www.picturethisai.com/region/tree/Israel-Tel-Aviv.html}} ==Cultivation == [[File:10 Shnongpdei 1.JPG|right|thumb|Aerial roots of ''Ficus elastica'' being formed into a bridge in [[Meghalaya]], India]] In parts of India, people guide the roots of the tree over chasms to eventually form [[living root bridges|living bridges]].{{Cite web |url=http://humanplanet.com/timothyallen/2011/03/living-root-bridges-bbc-human-planet/ |title=Living Root Bridges |date=21 March 2011 |access-date=2012-06-19 |archive-date=2018-06-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180621184459/http://humanplanet.com/timothyallen/2011/03/living-root-bridges-bbc-human-planet/ |url-status=live }} To this day there are large bridges woven from aerial roots in Meghalaya, India. Although the trees used for these bridges are very large, aerial roots can be found on ''F. elastica'' as small as 1 feet tall.{{Cite web |date=2022-06-21 |title=Do rubber trees have aerial roots? Yes! and people make living bridges with them!! |url=https://planthouseaesthetic.com/do-rubber-plants-have-aerial-roots-heres-what-you-need-to-know/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231004173242/https://planthouseaesthetic.com/do-rubber-plants-have-aerial-roots-heres-what-you-need-to-know/ |archive-date=2023-10-04 |website=Plant House Aesthetic}}{{Cite web |last=Mohanty |first=Trishna |title=In One of the Wettest Places on the Planet, Indigenous People Build Bridges and Ladders Out of Living Tree Roots |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/travel/in-one-of-the-wettest-places-on-the-planet-indigenous-people-build-bridges-and-ladders-out-of-living-tree-roots-180988405/ |access-date=2026-06-30 |website=Smithsonian Magazine |language=en}} == Use and production == Medicinal and nutritional usage of ''F. elastica'': a distillation of the plant's aerial rootlets can be used to make a poultice for healing wounds, while the tips of the leaves, when young, can be used as salad greens. Small versions of the trees can be grown as houseplants. ''F. elastica'' was once thought to improve indoor air quality when placed in the home;{{Cite web |title=ICIMOD |url=https://lml-database.icimod.org/detail/ficus-elastica#:~:text=Medicine%20%2D%20A%20decoction%20of%20the,used%20as%20an%20indoor%20plant.}} however, though ''F. elastica'' does remove 1 [[microgram]] per hour of [[formaldehyde]] from the air,Wolverton, B. C. (1996) ''How to Grow Fresh Air''. New York: Penguin Books. these results are not applicable to typical buildings, where outdoor-to-indoor air exchange already removes [[Volatile organic compound|volatile organic compounds (VOCs)]] at a rate that could only be matched by the placement of 10–1000 plants/m{{sup|2}} of a building's floor space.{{cite journal |last1=Cummings |first1=Bryan E. |last2=Waring |first2=Michael S. |title=Potted plants do not improve indoor air quality: a review and analysis of reported VOC removal efficiencies |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41370-019-0175-9 |journal=Journal of Exposure Science & Environmental Epidemiology |pages=253–261 |language=en |doi=10.1038/s41370-019-0175-9 |date=March 2020|volume=30 |issue=2 |pmid=31695112 |bibcode=2020JESEE..30..253C |s2cid=207911697 |url-access=subscription }} === Latex === All parts of the plant contain an abundant milky white [[latex]], a chemical compound separate from its sap and carried and stored in different [[laticifer|cells]]. The latex of ''F. elastica'' can irritate the eyes and skin, and is toxic if ingested.MacDonald, Elvin "The World Book of House Plants" Popular Books Its sap can be used to make [[rubber]]; it was once the most common plant in [[Sumatra]] and [[Malay Peninsula]] for tapping before the [[Hevea brasiliensis|Pará tree]] (''Hevea brasiliensis'') was introduced from Brazil in the late 1800s, and became the popular industrial cultivar thereafter.{{cite book |last=Barlow |first=Colin |year=1978 |title=The Natural Rubber Industry, Its Development, Technology, and Economy in Malaysia |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IsKzAAAAIAAJ&q=tapping+rambong |location=Petaling Jaya, Selangor, Malaysia |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=0-19-580314-0 |page=18}}{{Cite book |last=McCarthy |first=John F. |year=2006 |title=The Fourth Circle: A Political Ecology of Sumatra's Rainforest Frontier |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1jDdHY21JMAC&dq=tapping+rambung&pg=PA30 |location=Stanford, California, USA |publisher=Stanford University Press |page=30 |isbn=978-0-8047-5212-1}} ''F. elastica'' (known as Rambung trees) were very valuable to farmers in [[Aceh]] in Indonesia, who found them in their newly cleared lands. The latex of ''F. elastica'' has been tested for use in the manufacture of modern rubber, but without economic and technical results, due to the complications of tapping it, and its inferior yield when compared to ''Hevea brasiliensis''.{{Cite web |title=The Figs of Borneo: Ficus elastica: Cultivating the Rubber Plant |url=https://borneoficus.info/2019/06/19/ficus-elastica-cultivating-the-rubber-tree/}} ===Ornamental=== {{more citations needed section|date=May 2025}} ''F. elastica'' is grown around the world as an [[ornamental plant]]. It can be grown outside in frost-free climates ranging from tropical climates to the Mediterranean, and grown inside in colder climates as a houseplant. It is tolerant of light frosts, and thrives in [[USDA hardiness zone]]s 10–12.[https://www.gardenia.net/plant/ficus-elastica-rubber-tree Ficus elastica (Rubber Tree)] by Gardenia.net. Retrieved 1 May 2025. Although it is grown in Hawaii, the fig wasp species required for natural reproduction is not present there. In cultivation, it prefers bright sunlight but not hot temperatures. It has a high tolerance for drought, but prefers humidity and thrives in wet, tropical conditions. Ornamental [[hybrid (biology)|hybrid]]s (such as 'Robusta') have been derived from ''Fil. elastica'' with broader, stiffer and more upright leaves than the wild form. Many such hybrids exist, often with [[Variegation|variegated]] leaves. Most cultivated plants are produced by [[vegetative propagation]].
